posts.title: Blantyre’s bird lovers celebrate first ever show – November 1891
posts.description: Bird keeping was clearly a popular pastime in Victorian Blantyre. On Saturday 7th November 1891 , a newly established Ornithological Society held its very first bird show, attracting an impressive number of entries and proving a tremendous success. The event featured an amazing 200 entries , with canaries and other birds competing for prizes across several categories. The local newspaper reported that the show had been a great success, both financially and in the quality of birds exhibited. Organisers were so encouraged by the response that further events seemed certain to follow. Blantyre’s prize-winning birds! Among the highlights was a handsome yellow male canary belonging to Mr John Arbuckle of Blantyre , which won the chief award in the Scotch Fancy category, a beautiful silver cup! Meanwhile, Mr Love of Hamilton enjoyed a particularly successful day, winning the top award in the Norwich category with a magnificent dark-crested canary. posts.title: Blantyre Railway Station branded unfit for purpose – 1891
posts.description: Complaints about railway stations are certainly nothing new! Back in November 1891 , one frustrated commuter was publicly calling for major improvements to Blantyre Railway Station. Writing to the local newspaper under the name “A Daily Traveller” , the passenger criticised the Caledonian Railway Company for allowing the station to remain in such poor condition. The writer certainly didn’t hold back, declaring that the station buildings “would not make decent cattle sheds!” Not exactly a glowing review! The passenger argued that Blantyre had become a busy railway centre, yet the station facilities had failed to keep pace with the number of people using them. Two particular improvements were demanded. Wider platforms: The writer believed the existing platforms should be at least twice their current width to accommodate passengers safely. posts.title: Very suspicious parcel – Blantyre’s secret drinking habits in 1891
posts.description: It seems people in Victorian times were just as inventive as people today when it came to finding somewhere for a cheeky wee drink! An amusing newspaper story from November 1891 tells of some rather suspicious goings-on at the back of a grocery shop described as being “not a hundred miles from Blantyre”. The writer, known as “Salmagundi’s crony”, was standing in the shop when a very tall, well-built gentleman entered and asked the shopkeeper: “Is that parcel ready?” The shopkeeper gave him a knowing look and replied that it was. The burly customer promptly disappeared into the back shop, followed by the shopkeeper. Moments later, the shopkeeper returned, filled a small glass from a container marked 8d per gill , and disappeared into the back again! A short while later, the stocky customer emerged drying his lips on his sleeve and headed straight for the door, apparently having forgotten all about his mysterious parcel.
